paper_b.title: Stochastic Backpropagation and Approximate Inference in Deep Generative Models

metadata.description: Two essentially simultaneous (2014) and independent derivations of amortised stochastic variational inference for deep continuous-latent directed generative models. Both papers introduce a recognition network jointly trained with the generator, derive a reparameterised low-variance gradient estimator of the variational lower bound (Kingma-Welling: SGVB / 'reparameterization trick'; Rezende et al.: stochastic backpropagation via Bonnet/Price or location-scale reparameterisation), give the closed-form Gaussian KL, and demonstrate the resulting algorithm (AEVB / DLGM learning) on image benchmarks. The Rezende et al. paper additionally develops a hierarchical Gaussian latent model, a structured low-rank covariance, and a missing-data imputation Markov chain; the Kingma-Welling paper additionally treats fully Bayesian parameter inference and an importance-weighted marginal-likelihood estimator. The shared core makes this a textbook example of parallel rediscovery (PR).

matches.explanation: Both state the same problem: jointly learn the parameters of a directed continuous-latent generative model and obtain an approximate posterior, despite intractable marginals. Paper A frames it abstractly (ML/MAP + posterior + marginal for any p_theta(z) p_theta(x|z)); paper B specialises to the deep latent Gaussian model and writes it as free-energy minimisation, hence 'analogous' rather than 'exact'.

Paper A explicitly identifies the high-variance score-function (REINFORCE) gradient as a problem to be solved; paper B mentions REINFORCE only as a baseline in remarks and example (RP211.1, ExP211.5) but does not isolate it as a stated problem node.

Generative model definitions. Paper A defines a generic two-step continuous-latent directed model with a single latent z and decoder p_theta(x|z); paper B defines the Deep Latent Gaussian Model (DLGM), a hierarchical version with L Gaussian latent layers and the explicit recursion h_l = T_l(h_{l+1}) + G_l xi_l. Same conceptual role (the generative half of the model), but DLGM is a strict deep specialisation, so 'analogous'.

Both papers introduce the recognition model q_phi(z|x) (paper B writes q(xi|V, theta^r)) — an amortised data-conditioned approximate posterior parameterised by a neural network and learned jointly with the generator. This is the same object up to notation; paper B fixes the parametric family to a per-layer diagonal-plus-low-rank Gaussian, but the definition's role is identical.

Variational objective. Paper A's ELBO L(theta,phi;x) = -KL(q||p_theta(z)) + E_q[log p_theta(x|z)] (DP210.4) and the identity log p = KL + L (EP210.1, PrP210.2) coincide with paper B's free energy F(V) = KL[q||p] - E_q[log p(V|xi)] (DP211.3) — F = -ELBO up to a constant, with the same KL+reconstruction decomposition. EP211.3 gives the closed-form Gaussian instantiation, which is the same object expanded out. Match is mathematically exact (sign convention aside).

The reparameterisation trick / stochastic backpropagation. Paper A's 'reparameterization of latent variable' z = g_phi(eps,x) with eps independent of phi (DP210.5), the differentiable reparameterised expectation proposition (PrP210.1) and the underlying mild-differentiability assumption (AssumP210.1) are the same construction as paper B's 'Stochastic Backpropagation' (DP211.4) and its concrete reparameterisation gradient identity for xi = mu + R epsilon (TP211.3). This is the central shared contribution of the two papers.

Gaussian Backpropagation via Bonnet's and Price's theorems (TP211.1, TP211.2 — both external) is a Rezende et al.-specific contribution: an alternative derivative-of-Gaussian-density route to gradients of E_N(mu,C)[f] that is parallel to (and presented alongside) the location-scale reparameterisation. Paper A does not state or use Bonnet/Price; it relies solely on the change-of-variables route (PrP210.1). The two paper-origin appendix proofs PP211.1, PP211.2 (with their step decompositions) and the GBP definition/equation DP211.5, EP211.2 therefore have no Paper-A counterparts.

Both papers explicitly contrast their gradient estimator with the REINFORCE / score-function estimator. Paper A's EP210.2 writes the naive score-function gradient as a 'known to have very high variance' baseline and ProbP210.2 elevates the high-variance issue to a stated problem; paper B's AP211.3 cites Williams 1992 REINFORCE (with baseline) and then shows GBP variance is O(1) vs O(K). The cited estimator is the same object.

Paper A's 'Generic SGVB estimator (estimator A)' — a Monte Carlo estimate of the full integrand log p(x,z) - log q(z|x) under reparameterised samples — has no separately named counterpart in paper B, which only writes the closed-form Gaussian-KL form (paper B's analogue of estimator B).

KL-form / Gaussian SGVB estimator. Paper A's estimator B (EP210.4) and its concrete VAE Gaussian instantiation EP210.7 (1/2 sum (1+log sigma^2 - mu^2 - sigma^2) + 1/L sum log p(x|z)) are the same objective and gradient written in paper B as the closed-form free energy EP211.3 and its mu-/R-gradients EP211.4. Numerically identical up to sign and variable names.
Paper A's explicit minibatch SGVB estimator with the N/M scaling factor is not lifted to its own node in paper B; minibatching is mentioned only inside the algorithm pseudocode (ASP211.1).

Closed-form Gaussian-Gaussian KL between N(mu, sigma^2 I) and N(0,I), giving 1/2 sum (1 + log sigma^2 - mu^2 - sigma^2). Paper A states the result both as an equation (EP210.6) and as a proposition with assumptions and proof (PrP210.3, PP210.3). Paper B uses exactly the same identity inside its closed-form free energy EP211.3 (the [|mu|^2 + Tr C - log|C| - 1] block, generalised to full covariance).

Paper A's proof of the differentiable reparameterised estimator (change of variables + Monte Carlo) is asserted but not written out as a proof node in paper B; paper B's analogous proof material lives inside the Bonnet/Price appendix proofs (PP211.1, PP211.2) which take a different route. The L1-level parent therefore has no clean paper-B counterpart, and the L2 step DAGs are different enough that we omit a composite L2 entry per the v2 'parent skipped' rule.

Paper A's Appendix B proof of the Gaussian-Gaussian KL closed form (compute integral of q log p, integral of q log q, subtract) has no corresponding proof node in paper B — paper B simply writes the closed form inside the free energy EP211.3 without an explicit derivation node.

The importance-weighted marginal-likelihood estimator using HMC posterior samples (paper A's EP210.8 with derivation PP210.2) is a paper-A contribution for evaluating log p(x); paper B reports negative log-likelihoods on MNIST etc. but does not introduce or derive an analogous estimator as a node.

The flagship learning algorithm. Paper A's AEVB and paper B's 'Learning in DLGMs (Stochastic Backpropagation)' are the same procedure: initialise (theta, phi); loop over minibatches; sample from the recognition model with reparameterised noise; compute the gradient of the variational bound via reparameterisation; update both parameter sets with stochastic gradient (Adagrad in A, RMSprop in B). The compositions of L2 algorithm_steps line up step-for-step (sample minibatch, sample noise / bottom-up sample, compute reparameterised gradient, update parameters), so we treat the L1 parents as exact.

Composite L2 alignment of the inner algorithm steps of AP210.1 ↔ AP211.1. Paper A initialises parameters explicitly (ASP210.1) and has separate noise-sampling and minibatch-sampling steps (ASP210.3, ASP210.4); paper B folds initialisation into the algorithm preamble and combines noise sampling with the bottom-up recognition pass (ASP211.2). Both have an explicit gradient-computation step (ASP210.5 ↔ ASP211.4), an SGD/RMSprop update (ASP210.6 ↔ ASP211.5), and an outer convergence loop (ASP210.2/ASP210.7 ↔ ASP211.6). Granularity differs, hence 'analogous'.

Paper A's full-VB stochastic-gradient procedure (AP210.2), placing a variational posterior on the generative parameters theta themselves with a second reparameterisation theta = h_phi(zeta), has no counterpart in paper B, which keeps theta^g as point estimates with an L2 prior (the |theta^g|^2/(2 kappa) term in EP211.3).

Both papers cite Hinton et al. 1995 wake-sleep as the principal prior algorithm for training directed latent-variable models with a recognition network. Origin = external on both sides; the underlying algorithm is identical, so this is a high-confidence external↔external match. Per the v2 prompt, this carries no signal for relation_type.
Paper A's Monte Carlo EM with HMC baseline algorithm is external-origin and has no paper-B counterpart (paper B's comparison baselines are wake-sleep, NADE, DBN, RBM rather than MCEM/HMC).

Rank-one-plus-diagonal precision parameterisation C^{-1} = D + u u^T (DP211.6) and the explicit closed-form R factor (EP211.5) are paper-B-specific scalability contributions. Paper A uses a fully diagonal Gaussian recognition model, so there is no corresponding structured-covariance node.

Paper B's missing-data imputation via a recognition Markov chain (algorithm AP211.2) and the supporting L1 fixed-point bound (PrP211.1, with proof PP211.3) are an entire paper-B-specific application track absent from paper A. Their L2 step children are implicitly unmatched per the compactness rule.

Paper B cites the fundamental theorem for Markov chains (Neal 1993) only inside the imputation appendix; with no imputation chain on the paper-A side, there is no symmetric external citation to align to.

Concrete neural-network instantiations of the abstract model. Paper A defines the 'Variational Auto-Encoder' (DP210.6) with Bernoulli-MLP and Gaussian-MLP encoder/decoder choices (DP210.7, DP210.8). Paper B's 'Two-Layer DLGM Activation' example (ExP211.1) plays the same role for its hierarchical model: an explicit MLP-style instantiation with a low-rank-Gaussian recognition network. Same conceptual contribution (concrete network architecture), different schema slot (definition vs example) and different generator topology, hence 'analogous'.
